speech: Itchy skin at night can be a sign of something worse.
Watch this before you buy another tube of cream.
She came to see me the other day. She's 66.
She didn't think she had allergies, but her skin had been giving her a lot of trouble.
Every night, when she got into bed, it started.
Her arms, her neck, the backs of her legs.
Some nights, she'd scratch until it burned.
But during the day, her skin would calm down.
She often wake up scratching,
and by morning, her nose was blocked and her eyes were puffy.
One night, she slept on the couch and the itching stopped.
This had been going on for quite a long time, and she'd had enough.
She was ready to find out what was going on.
Her doctor had already checked her skin.
Overall, nothing too impressive.
A little dryness, a little irritation, nothing unusual for her age.
But with her symptoms, I had a sneaky suspicion I knew what was going on.
So I showed her what lives inside a mattress, and it looks a little something like this.
A mattress like hers can hold anywhere from 100,000 to 10 million dust mites.
What does this mean?
Basically, dust mites live in the fabric of your mattress,
where they feed on the skin you shed every night.
Every mite leaves about 20 droppings a day, loaded with an allergen called Derpy One.
And you lie in it for eight hours a night.
This can build up for a few reasons.
An older mattress, a warm humid bedroom, years of shed skin packed into the fabric.
Some homes are just more humid than others.
Either way, it explained why everything was worst for her in bed.
We looked at her options.
There are antihistamines and creams for relief.
There's replacing the mattress, but a new one starts filling right back up from your pillows
and your own skin within a few months.
But ultimately, the best thing to do is get them out of the mattress with capture cards.
Dust mites have no eyes.
They follow scent.
Capture cards give off a plant-derived pheromone lure that reaches into the fabric they hide in
and pulls them onto the card, where the adhesive holds them.
It doesn't kill them where they are, because a dead mite carries the same allergen as a live one.
It brings them out.
For comparison, sprays and vacuums only reached the top layer.
She was skeptical, understandably, after dealing with this for so long.
But she gave it a real shot before buying a new mattress.
One card under the mattress, one near her pillow, when she came back six weeks later.
She told me that itching at night had noticeably eased.
Her mornings were clearer.
She was sleeping better too.
She said she wished she'd found it sooner.
